transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-19
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 63 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Ethan Park (Redwood SE); Lina Alvarez (Redwood Infra SE); Alex Marin (Hypatia CTO); Priya Rao (Hypatia ML Eng); Jonas Becker (Hypatia Infra); Sara Nguyen (Hypatia Security)
Shared: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/128k-stride (redwood internal), Hypatia-sample-trace-2026-10-12.log (customer link)

Summary:
Hypatia wants to run generative assistants with ~150k average conversation context, occasional 500k+ append for legal docs. Primary constraints: 200ms p95 latency SLO for interactive features, hard data residency (on-prem/VPC), and audit logs for SOC2. Discussed strided/sparse attention patterns, windowed KV tiering, eviction policies, and batching/quantization tradeoffs. Agreed to run a pilot with dedicated nodes and provide traces.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): yeah hi everyone thanks for joining, quick intro, I'm Maya, Ethan will do the deep runtime bits, Lina will touch infra options. Alex from Hypatia?
[00:12] Alex (Hypatia): hi yeah Alex here, thanks. we run a doc assistant used by legal ops, most conversations are long, we often append whole contracts so context grows fast. target is ~200ms p95 for short queries and acceptable tail for very long appends.
[00:28] Ethan (Redwood SE): great, so high-level, for 128k plus we split into chunking layers + KV caching. we've been experimenting with strided attention and windowed KV tiers to keep active tokens hot.
[00:40] Priya (Hypatia): can you explain stride attention again? I read about it but not sure how it affects latency with small batch sizes.
[00:48] Ethan: sure. strided attention means you attend densely within local blocks and use strided/global tokens for cross-block communication. so compute drops from O(n^2) naive for long sequences to something like O(n * window) plus some cross-block overhead. the tradeoff is slight quality drop unless you tune the stride and add overlap.
[01:12] Jonas (Hypatia): what's the overlap size you guys usually find works? 1-2k?
[01:18] Ethan: we often do 4-8k overlap for 128k context setups but that depends on model and prompt patterns. more importantly is KV cache locality - if your hot set is in a recent window, hits are high and effective latency stays low.
[01:32] Maya: quick callout — Hypatia, you mentioned legal docs and append-heavy workloads; that profile favors aggressive prefix pruning and multi-tier KV (hot/near-cold/cold) vs full keep-all.
[01:44] Priya: what are the eviction heuristics? LRU? time-based?
[01:49] Lina (Redwood Infra SE): we use hybrid heuristics: recency-weighted LRU with pinned segments for active sessions. in Dedicated and Private deployments we allow a local SSD-backed near-cold tier and a remote blob cold tier. hot tier stays in GPU memory (KV cache), near-cold in NVMe attached to the same host, cold in object store.
[02:05] Alex: and eviction under throughput spikes? we have bursty ingestion when batches of scanned docs land.
[02:12] Ethan: we implement backpressure -> graceful degradation: if KV miss rate spikes, we can fallback to a lower-cost sparse attention variant or route to a smaller model version to keep latency SLOs. fallback policies are configurable per-customer.
[02:25] Priya: question: how do you reconcile batching (for cost) and a 200ms p95 SLO? our interactive UI needs quick responses.
[02:34] Ethan: yeah that's classic. batching improves throughput but increases latency. we use adaptive batching windows — short windows for interactive routes (e.g., 10-50ms) and longer for background jobs. in practice we set a max batch delay of 20ms for interactive to hit p95, and then rely on KV hit-rate to reduce per-token compute.
[02:52] Jonas: and quantization — we want smaller memory footprint on our on-prem cards. how safe is 4-bit quant for long context?
[02:58] Lina: quantization introduces some degradation. our recommendations: 8-bit for most, 4-bit QAT only after evals on your prompt set. for heavy long-context ops, mixed precision (kv keys in FP16, weights in 4-bit where possible) often preserves behavior. testing is key.
[03:17] Sara (Security): we need to confirm KMS integration for on-prem HSM, and audit log retention. how does Dedicated vs Private change that?
[03:24] Maya: Dedicated is still Redwood-managed infra but isolated; Private is customer-managed control plane with VPC connectors and can integrate with your KMS/HSM. audit logs and longer retention are an add-on. we'll share SOC2 / ISO artifacts.
[03:36] Alex: can we go deeper on windowed KV ops — like the exact eviction thresholds and how you pin segments for active threads?
[03:43] Ethan: sure. example: for a 128k session we partition context into 4k segments. active window = last 32k (8 segments) pinned in GPU KV. next 64k in near-cold NVMe, accessible with async prefetch, and oldest 32k in cold object store. eviction threshold is dynamic: when GPU KV usage exceeds 90% we start demoting least-recently-referenced segments, but we also track session affinity so we avoid demoting pinned segments for ongoing dialogs.
[04:11] Priya: what about prefetch jitter causing tail latency spikes?
[04:16] Ethan: we observed that naive prefetch caused microbursts. solution: staggered prefetch with bandwidth caps and coalesced IO, plus predictive prefetch based on session access patterns. also, we limit concurrent prefetch per GPU to avoid IO saturation.
[04:30] Jonas: curious how kernel selection affects long sequences; do you pick different kernels for strided vs dense attention?
[04:36] Ethan: yes; runtime chooses kernels based on architecture, sequence length distribution, and attention pattern. for strided we use sparse attention kernels optimized for indexing, for local windows we use fused attention kernels with better memory locality. this is part of our compilation step.
[04:50] Alex: any numbers you can share on p95 improvement with hot KV + 20ms batch window vs naive dense attention?
[04:57] Ethan: rough numbers from our internal bench: for a 128k workload with 8k overlap, hot KV hit-rate ~85% yields token latency ~6-8ms/token and p95 end-to-end ~180-220ms with 20ms batching. naive dense attention would be multiple seconds per request at those lengths. note: numbers vary by model size and GPU generation.
[05:18] Priya: model size — we're evaluating 13B vs 70B. how does that change approach?
[05:23] Ethan: smaller models have lower per-token compute but worse long-range understanding sometimes. from runtime perspective, 13B occupies less KV footprint so you can keep larger hot windows; 70B needs careful KV tiering and more NVMe prefetching. also kernel availability differs — some fused kernels are more optimized for certain dims.
[05:41] Maya: side note — for on-prem we can offer a hybrid where the control plane is private and we ship a compact inference runtime container you run; Redwood still provides kernel updates and rollout.
[05:52] Sara: with hybrid, what happens to logs? do they leave our VPC?
[05:56] Lina: logs can be fully retained in-customer VPC and only minimal telemetry sent (opt-in). we support S3-compatible object stores for cold KV and integrate with your SIEM for audit logs.
[06:08] Alex: are there any pitfalls in using strided attention with long legal text — do you lose cross-reference resolution?
[06:15] Ethan: good question. stride patterns can miss some distant dependencies. techniques to mitigate: overlapping windows, global tokens for citation anchors, and reranking stage where a smaller subset of candidates is rescored with denser attention. also we run targeted evals on your prompt sets to quantify regressions.
[06:34] Priya: can you walk through a sample request lifecycle with our profile? like a user opens doc, asks question with 150k context.
[06:40] Ethan: yeah. request lifecycle: 1) request comes in -> route to interactive model pool (short batching window). 2) runtime checks session KV in GPU memory; if miss, async prefetch NVMe segments (prefetch policy may add 10-30ms) but if miss and latency tight, runtime falls back to sparse-stride mode to maintain SLO. 3) generation happens using local fused kernels and KV lookups; post-process includes citation extraction and audit log wrote. 4) if content requires deep cross-document reasoning, we optionally enqueue a background dense pass for improved answer and to update session embedding cache.
[07:12] Jonas: what's the typical hit-rate for near-cold NVMe prefetch to be useful?
[07:17] Ethan: depends a lot, but if access locality is >60% then NVMe prefetch pays off; below that you end up thrashing. we instrument access patterns to tune segment size and prefetch depth.
[07:27] Alex: ok good. question about quantization again — do you keep KV in FP16 regardless of weight quant?
[07:33] Ethan: we recommend KV in FP16 (or BF16) to preserve representation; weights can be 4-bit or 8-bit. keeping KV higher precision reduces compounding errors across long sequences.
[07:45] Priya: data residency for cold tier — can you store cold on our on-prem object store?
[07:50] Lina: yes that's a supported Private option — cold tier can be customer-managed S3-compatible store in VPC. runtime will only access via private networking.
[07:58] Sara: any formal attestations we can use for procurement?
[08:01] Maya: we'll share SOC2 report and an architecture whitepaper for Private deployment; procurement typically needs an SOW — we'll circulate a template.
[08:10] Ethan: quick note on batch sizing experiments: for your p95 target we recommend experiments at batch delays 10, 20, 50ms and measuring p50/p95/p99. also try different segment sizes (2k/4k/8k) to find the best KV locality tradeoff.
[08:26] Priya: do you have any example config for eviction thresholds?
[08:29] Ethan: yes — typical starting config: hot-gpu cap 90%; pinned window size 32k; near-cold depth 64k; prefetch depth 2 segments; demote rate 50ms per eviction event; these are all tunable. we'll share a starter config.
[08:43] Alex: are there any known memory fragmentation issues with long-context continuous sessions?
[08:48] Lina: fragmentation can occur if you pin many small segments; remedy: coalesce segments periodically and compact KV layout during low traffic windows. compaction windows are scheduled automatically.
[08:58] Jonas: what's the rollback story if a kernel update regresses perf?
[09:01] Ethan: runtime supports canary rollouts and pinning to previous kernels; Dedicated deployments can pin until you approve an update. our rollout system also runs perf tests in a staging pool.
[09:14] Priya: okay last question — how invasive is the on-prem install? we have restricted change windows and strict firewall rules.
[09:20] Lina: install is containerized. for Private we provide an operator and limited privileged containers. network wise you can opt for fully air-gapped with manual license sync if needed. we have docs for both.
[09:32] Maya: wrap up and next steps — we'll send the benchmark sheet, starter configs, and SOC2 artifacts. Hypatia to send traces and target latency percentiles. plan to reconvene to scope pilot.
[09:45] Alex: thanks everyone, this was useful.
[09:48] Priya: thanks.
[09:49] Maya: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
